https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Why I won’t stop hunting with hounds
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Imagine being launched into a land of myth: a place where man and beast merge, where mind and nature meet. This, the late philosopher Roger Scruton suggests in a paean to the foxhunting that became his great passion, is a realm towards which riding to hounds — “an unselfconscious union between species, which [is] also a rejoicing in the land” — can lead you. An integral element of rural culture, hunting brings creature and countryside and community together, he argues, in a way that is not only glorious but good.
Hunting, though, is also a blood sport. Its atavistic traditions are decried as brutal. Can it really be condoned by our modern world? It certainly rouses fiercely antipathetic passions, which is why, for fear of reprisal from hunt saboteurs, I and several of the people that I have interviewed for this piece feel safer remaining anonymous.
Twenty years have elapsed since the passing of the 2004 Hunting Act under Tony Blair’s Labour government. It banned the chasing of wild mammals with dogs. But certain alternatives or exemptions are permitted and, where previously a fox would have been flushed out of a covert and pursued across country to be killed by a pack of hounds, now only trail hunting — the tracking of a previously laid scent, a pungent cocktail of strong-smelling stuff made of anything from animal urine to aniseed — is allowed.
After two decades you might expect any new law to have settled into acceptance. Not this one. A piece of legislation that, in its planning, threw our country out of kilter, instigating the biggest rural protest that our nation has ever seen (407,791 people converged on the capital in the 2002 countryside marches) now looks set to start stirring up turmoil again.
A general election is on the horizon and Labour is keen to claw back a lost rural vote. “Under Blair we had more than 100 rural seats,” the Labour peer Baroness Ann Mallalieu explains . “Now only about 17.”
“I want everyone in the countryside to know that I will roll up my sleeves and restore respect,” Sir Keir Starmer has said. At the same time, however, he is building his own stumbling block. He is looking to reopen the issue of hunting, to bring forward new laws that will “strengthen” an act that, two decades ago, prohibited it. That might seem to the majority like a pretty niche matter, not to mention unnecessary — how can you ban something that has already been banned? But to tens of thousands of rural dwellers it might prove a deciding factor, because now even trail hunting is facing a possible ban.
There is a growing consensus in the agricultural community that, in our post-Brexit era, it could be well served by Labour with its promises of access to cheap, clean energy, fewer food imports and a veterinary agreement with the EU. And yet, in the run-up to an election, other country people are already rallying behind the Conservatives — for one simple reason. A farming neighbour in the West Country explains it: “We don’t want a ban on [trail] hunting. We don’t want a stop to what is our life.” As this year’s hunting season draws to its close, many are beginning to fear that it might have been their very last.
I hunted as a child. It was something that kids who grew up in the countryside did. Besides, I had seen the sad, mange-infected foxes and persuaded myself that it was kinder to dispatch them — not that, on my fat little pony, I was ever anywhere near enough to the front to be in at the kill. But then teenage qualms about animal cruelty set in. I became a vegetarian — and no doubt fantastically self-righteous to boot. Then came A-levels, university, a job in London. I barely got the chance to get on a horse any more, let alone go hunting — and by the time I had returned to my rural roots, the Hunting Act had been passed.
I returned to riding to hounds about ten years ago. I’m a member of a West Country trail hunt: one of the 170 or so packs of foxhounds that still operate in the UK — though there are also stag, basset and bloodhounds, harriers and beagles as well as rarer minkhound and Sealyham packs.
A day out starts early. I rise in the darkness to call my horse in from the valley. I hose, brush and polish him from muddied ear tips to oiled hooves. Then, once I’ve fitted his newly cleaned tack, I hurry inside to pull on my own togs: layers of modern thermals beneath traditional breeches, long boots and coat, finished off with an old-fashioned, finger-fuddling stock tie. The last is sometimes said to stop your neck from breaking. But I can tell you it doesn’t work — I broke my neck out hunting a few years ago.
Stuffing my field money into a pocket — members subscribe annually but pay a small additional sum each time they go out, which goes towards staff salaries and care of the hunt’s horses and hounds — and, racing about frantically to find that missing glove, I set off, sometimes in a trailer; sometimes on horseback.
The meet is the melting pot of the rural community. Forget the “unspeakable in full pursuit of the uneatable” cliché. Quite apart from the fact that a fox stewed with thyme and ginger can make a fine dinner, most people who ride to hounds are far from posh. “I would guess that 80 per cent of our followers earn less than the huntsman,” a master of foxhounds from the West Country tells me. “They’re probably on about £20,000 a year. They’ll never go on holiday. A horse is their one luxury. They’ll keep it on the farm and look after it themselves. Hunting is the backbone of everything they know.”
“The ’unt? … Well, it’s life, innum,” an old shepherd says. “Oh, ’tis. ’Tis part and parcel,” his wife adds. A significant sector of the rural economy — livery yards, farriers, saddlers, grooms, vets, horse breeders and trainers, equine dentists and osteopaths — depends on the hunt. Its social activities — point-to-points, hunter trials, Pony Club; breakfasts, barbecues and balls; fun rides and farmers’ suppers; not to mention the St Hubert’s Day service, carols at Christmas and the vicar’s annual blessing of the hounds — lie at the core of a rural social life.
The generations mix at the meet. “The hunt looks after us from birth to death,” one rider tells me: a digger driver, as it turns out, who on Saturday mornings swaps his JCB for a piebald cob. Toddlers cling on to the tufty manes of tiny ponies. Teenagers chatter with veterans. And an important part of the job, one huntsman explains, is to turn up at funerals, where they blow the plangent Gone Away at the graveside.
Everyone mills about in a mêlée of good-mornings and doffed caps. They swap local gossip and, if it’s a lawn meet — traditionally hosted in front of some mansion but more likely a muddy farmyard — there will be pasties, roast potatoes and port.
The horses fidget impatiently. The hunter, unlike many equines, does not have to spend its life circling round and around an arena. Fit and well fed, it does what horses love most — it gallops free (or at least relatively free) with the herd.
As the hounds pour from their transport lorry, cocking legs on car tyres and pinching the odd sausage, the horses snort, stamp and spin. The huntsman (this is the person who works the hounds), standing quietly on the fringes, summons his pack. He knows each hound by name. He could tell you their pedigrees right back to the 1700s. He feeds them on a diet of raw flesh (an important role of the hunt is to pick up fallen stock for the farmers). He cleans out their kennels every morning and last thing at night it is he who will tuck them into bed.
Sometimes at the end of the day he might be spotted alone in the middle of nowhere, waiting for the return of some laggard. Once, a huntsman tells me, he had to drive 250 miles to retrieve one of his hounds. A pair of holidaymakers, assuming it to be abandoned, had bundled it into their car and taken it home. It was only a week later, when they took it to training classes because it was so depressed, that they finally discovered their new pet, far from being unwanted, was a treasured foxhound.
The huntsman of my pack knows roughly, he tells me, where the trail — laid an hour or so earlier by dragging a scent-drenched rag from the back of a quad bike — will begin. But not precisely. He wants his hounds to have to work: to use the instinct bred into them for centuries rather than allowing them to depend on him for a lead. “It’s like a police inquiry,” he explains. “They know nothing, then they find a little clue and that sends them off — hopefully — in the right direction.” If they pick up a live scent he can summon them back to him instantly by blowing his horn.
Hunt masters have been busy on the telephone the night before a day out. They have been clearing the country: chatting to farmers whose land they intend to cross, finding out if the ground might be too wet for horses or in which particular fields the pregnant ewes are kept. The hunt depends on the goodwill of its landowners. If a fence or a gate gets broken, it will be repaired by the hunt the very next day. Followers who transgress the rules — out of carelessness or ignorance — are severely reprimanded.
The riders wait. Clouds scud over landscapes that a motor-borne traveller will traverse and never discover but which, when crossed on horseback, immerses you in its rise and fall, in its windblown expanses and its branch-tangled crevices, in its patchworks of scrub and spreads of old turf. Perhaps you notice the crows as they buffet, claw-to-beak. Maybe you smell the wet grass, feel the coldness of rain as it rolls down your cheeks. You are not just an onlooker; you are a participant. This is what I love the most.
The hounds bound about like happy hooligans. How glad they seem compared with their urban cousins, which, bred with backs stretched to breaking point or snouts that can’t breathe, endure cosseted existences on the end of a lead. Who could feel miserable watching hounds work?
Suddenly a single hound will speak: a tremulous song of a note. It is galumphing away, nose low to the trail, and the rest of the pack, translated in an instant from excitable yobs to disciplined professionals, falls into line. They are off. The field does its utmost to keep up. But horse followers, to be frank, are not necessary. They just come along for the ride. In some parts of the country they will leap hedges, ditches and walls. Where I am, it’s more about tussocky hilltops and plunging slopes. Necks stretching, tails streaming, gobs of mud and sweat flying, we hurtle: horse, hound and human united, uplifted, inebriated by joy.
I’ve seen plenty of foxes. I’ve watched them slinking to safety along the edges of copses. I’ve seen them patrolling my hedgerows as protective ewes stamp. At dusk they sneak round my yard in the hopes of finding a stray hen. I’ve lost the odd goose when she’s nested too far afield and I’ve given up on call ducks — they merely served as a vulpine brand of KitKat. But since I began trail hunting I’ve never seen a fox killed by hounds — not even the one that dashed between my horse’s legs one morning. It turned sharp right into some nearby farm buildings. I held my breath. The hounds, streaming by shortly afterwards, turned sharp left along the trail.
The League Against Cruel Sports (LACS) informs me otherwise. “Trail-hunting is just a smokescreen behind which the killing of foxes takes place,” its spokesman says. Anyone who cares about the welfare of animals will certainly wince at the videos that can be found on the internet. There have undoubtedly been a handful of deliberate and brutal transgressions, not to mention a few unfortunate accidents when the hounds came by chance across a hapless fox. But does that mean that all riding to hounds should be banned?
In the face of the many greater and far graver problems that our natural world faces — climate change that pushes entire species towards extinction, the appalling degradation of our soils, factory farming that imprisons animals in misery — the strength of feeling that this issue rouses seems nothing if not idiosyncratic. Even Tony Blair, whose government passed the act, found himself perplexed. “One of the strangest parts of politics is how you get into situations of unbelievable controversy without ever meaning to or wanting to,” he said in his 2010 memoir. “The foxhunting subject resulted in one of the domestic legislative measures I most regret.” Why? Because it was “the cause of inordinate political convulsion, and for what purpose, God only knows.”
“The rules need to be tightened up,” the LACS spokesman says . “Greater penalties must be put into place to properly deter people.” He estimates that about 25 to 30 convictions for the chasing and killing of foxes have been brought in the past 20 years but he believes there have been many more infringements — just without sufficient evidence to bring them to court. (Official figures compiled by Labour in 2022 showed that at least 438 convictions have been secured under the act since 2010.)
Long-held habits can be too slow to change, suggests Ivan Massow, a master of foxhounds. “My heart breaks every time I read that another hunt has broken the law,” he says. “I see it as another nail in the coffin for what in all other respects is a perfectly well-behaved occupation. But thankfully the fact that there are increasingly fewer incidents shows that few are doing it.”
I ask him about the notorious Hankinson trial in 2021: a landmark case that stemmed from the leak of a series of training webinars in which senior figures from the hunting community appeared to admit that trail hunting could be used as a smokescreen. Hankinson was found guilty, but his conviction was overturned on appeal.
“That f***ing Mark Hankinson,” is Massow’s unrestrained response. “I can’t believe he did that. Though the irony is that he has probably done trail hunting a favour through his ineptitude. He has blown it open and made the killing of live quarry impossible. Before, it didn’t seem possible to reform the Masters of Foxhounds Association (MFHA) because it was full of stubbornly old-fashioned people. Now this has finally swept them all out.”
A new type of follower is emerging for whom the riding is the main pleasure, explains Andrew German, huntsman of the High Peak Harriers in Derbyshire. “My field is mostly people who just want to have a nice day out on a horse with lots of jumps. A new generation are growing up who have never known ‘proper’ hunting and are happy to see it just as an equine sport.”
“We never transgress the law,” he adds. When, in 2020, his pack accidentally killed someone’s cat while out on a walk, the apologies issued were profuse — though I can’t help but remember the study in 2022 that estimated that 270 million creatures, a quarter of them birds, are killed every year in this country by our beloved feline pets.
The disjuncture gapes. We are becoming screened off from our natural world. We watch it through car windows or on television sets. But even the presenter Chris Packham recently whipped up a furore when Winterwatch showed a deer’s carcass decomposing. Outraged viewers professed themselves sickened at the sight, unable to eat their sofa suppers. The red in tooth and claw does not make a palatable accompaniment to the ready meal. Hunting is condemned as reprehensible.
“If you are going to manage wildlife, you should do it in the least cruel way possible,” the LACS says.
If it’s animal welfare that concerns us, it’s probably time to give hunting another close look. According to a recently published book, Rural Wrongs by Charlie Pye-Smith, the passing of the Hunting Act has resulted in a drastic decline of British wildlife. The book was co-researched by Jim Barrington, a former director of the League Against Cruel Sports, who is now convinced that hunting can do good. In the uplands, for instance, where hounds are often the only feasible means of vulpine control, fox numbers have rocketed, to the detriment of ground-nesting birds. Meanwhile, in the lowlands, newer technologies such as night vision-enabled rifles and GPS mapping leave even fewer foxes than before the ban.
Farmers would once have tolerated and even protected this animal because, thanks to hunting, it was integral to their way of life. “Lots of hunting people live on farms,” an Exmoor man tells me. “They probably work with their family, probably only their dad, and they never get out. The one place I can socialise and talk and escape from the pressures of the farm is when I go hunting. Then, for once, you’re not worrying about your loan that’s come up, or the finance on your machine. You’re just away, you are. Away from it all.”
It is as deceptive to anthropomorphise an animal as it is to deny the animal in ourselves and our will to survive at the cost of other creatures. “Even the action of ploughing a field, turning it over to produce food for vegans, is genocide,” Massow points out. “Every mouse, frog and snake, and eventually even the precious soil bacteria, will die.”
For those whose concern is the balance of nature, it begins to be arguable that this balance is maintained by the hunt. The lives of man and beast are linked: the hunt helps our wild populations to stay healthy and hunting keeps our human communities strong too. And it is not some mythical dream that will vanish with its banning. It is a vital reality of our rural world.
The Hunting Act, which was passed by Labour 20 years ago, bans chasing and killing wild mammals with dogs in England and Wales. There are exemptions in the legislation for certain types of pest control or scientific research, and animal rights campaigners say trail hunts exploit these loopholes to circumvent the ban and kill live foxes with little concern for prosecution. Hounds, they argue, can pick up a live fox scent and accompanying terrier men will send their dogs underground to trap a fox while they dig it out and then shoot it. The League Against Cruel Sports says hunts can wreak havoc by marauding through farms, worrying and killing livestock or pets.
